Here are 5 popular reasons people give for why buy/use Bitcoin (or rather, bagHODL shitcoins, since nobody fucking buys them/wants them now):

  1. “It’s anonymous or pseudonymous..“ Since mining is no longer an option for the common man, you must now use an exchange to get Bitcoins. Exchanges are centralized and can never be decentralized (since it is logically impossible to ‘decentralize’ fiat/actual money). Thus they come under the unavoidable influence of national governments, who can (and do) demand strict identity verification procedures, checks to be made and records to be kept. Bitcoin 'ATMs’ have even gone a step further and require biometric data, such as fingerprints. Even if you were to pay a highly inflated premium and acquire Bitcoins through a black-market such as localbitcoins (and assuming you don’t get caught in a sting operation, as has already occurred several times), your purchase of assets will be your undoing - in tax law for instance you are guilty until proven innocent, and if the tax office notice you’ve got a brand new Lamborghini parked outside your house and registered in your name, they might send you a polite letter asking you to account for the fact, when as far as they know, you only work an underpaid part-time job.

  2. “It’s feeless or has low fees..” When you buy Bitcoin you have to pay both spread and exchange fees, and if it’s to be cashed out later, that goes double. We have heard about this promise of Bitcoin’s globalism, yet national borders remain embedded in the Bitcoin price - It is more expensive for instance to convert to or from Bitcoin on Australian exchanges, than in the US or in Europe. This was inevitable though, because whatever money can be squeezed out, will be squeezed out, and so this promise of 'globalism’ is naive and false. To convert from USD to Bitcoin, and then from Bitcoin to AUD, it costs more (in both time and money) than traditionally sending and converting from USD to AUD through Paypal. Even fees within Bitcoin itself are a pending disaster, for if fees are not increased massively in line with transaction growth, then nodes will become overburdened by bandwidth requirements as the blockchain becomes bloated, and the network will either become severely bottle-necked and effectively come to a standstill, or the network will literally go offline, as nodes start turning off (only a few thousand remain as of now). Either transactions must be artificially limited, or fees must greatly increase - and neither choice bodes well for the future viability of the network.

  3. “It allows merchants and buyers (i.e. 'Me!’) to save money..” As someone who sells a few things here and there, I know precisely why this intuition is certainly false. I would love to be able to offer a discount because of Bitcoin, because I would undercut all my competition. Problem is, if I can offer the discount, what stops them from doing the same? And once everybody offers the same discount, it ceases being a discount or advantage. People don’t actually care about saving peanuts anyway. Just look at Apple and you’ll recognize that people don’t mind what they pay in reality; they care about feeling good about what they buy. Discounts and 'sales’ tap into this motivation, because what makes you feel good is that you think you’re getting a rare and special deal - not that you’ve saving 1.4% or $0.35. So this whole thing about Bitcoin providing discounts is an illusion, because it doesn’t change the balance of competition; it doesn’t change the cost of the supply of goods.

  4. “It will make me get rich quick..” The Willy Report proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the two bubbles in 2013 were the work of insider trading at MtGox, buying up hundreds of millions of dollars worth of Bitcoins on the open market with a balance made up out of thin air. Karpeles was probably also behind the 2011 bubble, considering he was already a convicted fraud who fled France to Japan to escape jail, and then bought MtGox off Jeb Caleb one month before the 2011 bubble. Now that MtGox is gone, there is no reason to believe there will be another great bubble, and the price so far supports that hypothesis.

  5. “It’s a social revolution worthy of my support..” Look at the top knobs in Bitcoin right now. The most prominent ones, if you don’t want to think of it as a hierarchy. The 'space’ is infested with thugs, frauds and sociopaths. Karpeles, Shrem, Ver, Zhou Tong/Ryan Zhou or whatever name he goes by nowadays.. they’re all convicted frauds. 'Lukejr’ is an ideologue, Brewster (of Neo&Bee) was perhaps naive but nonetheless a fraud, Antonopoulos is perhaps also in the same category (note his involvements in Neo&Bee and Blockchain.info), Theymos is not yet convicted but his guilt is no doubt evident to even most Bitcoiners. Same with Garza and to a lesser extent the drug-addled fiend behind 'Sean’s Outpost’ (lookup Jason King’s previous 'ScrollQuest’ fraud if you think he’s just a naive do-gooder victim). The 'Bitcoin Foundation’, a self-proclaimed authority, attracts all manner of sociopaths including child molesters (Brock Pierce) as well as liars (anyone observing the recent shit-flinging over the 'minutes’ will know this). It’s not just immoral, it’s also inefficient - The Bitcoin Foundation, Bitpay, etc. are all on the verge of Bankruptcy. Neo&Bee and countless exchanges have already gone under. Mostly due to staggeringly stupid decisions, such as Neo&Bee’s primetime ads on televised Football matches, or Bitpay’s 'Bitcoin bowl’ stunt, or Theymos and his million dollar forum. Ask yourself: Is this a change from the traditional system? Has Bitcoin taken away the element of 'corruption’ or 'inefficiency’? Is this what you want to support?

We now can not only theorize, but know through the demonstration of fact that Bitcoin is inherently susceptible to:

  1. Fraud
  2. Fees
  3. Price manipulation
  4. State Regulation
  5. Corruption and bureaucratic inefficiency

The barbarians are not at the gates - they’re already well and truly inside, the gates being wide open to them. And it wasn’t that anyone held these gates open, but that Bitcoin itself is not a protected closed-loop system.

Bitcoin is just Paypal 2.0; a shittier version that nonetheless generates a lot of excitement, despite the fact that it’s Big Brother’s wet dream since every transaction is recorded for all to see (even if you bought a hotdog off a beach-side stand).
